analysis.one_liner: Bars doctors from charging Medicare patients membership or extra fees as a condition of care Medicare already covers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred doctors from charging Medicare patients membership fees to receive covered services, was referred to two House committees in June 2003 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicare to stop doctors and other practitioners from charging seniors a membership or other extra fee — or making them buy non-covered items — before providing care that Medicare already covers. Doctors who knowingly did this could face sanctions, including being kept out of Medicare for up to two years. The idea was to keep the growing practice of concierge-style membership fees from becoming a toll seniors had to pay just to get care they had earned through Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — primarily seniors and people with disabilities — gain a guarantee that they cannot be charged a membership fee or forced to buy non-covered items or services as a condition of receiving care Medicare already pays for. Doctors who do not charge such fees also benefit from a level playing field, since they cannot be undercut by practices that effectively require an extra subscription to see a patient.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits doctors and other practitioners from requiring Medicare beneficiaries to pay a membership or other incidental fee as a condition of receiving care that Medicare already covers.
It also prohibits practitioners from forcing Medicare patients to buy non-covered items or services as a condition of getting covered care.
It gives the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to sanction doctors who knowingly and willfully violate the ban, including excluding them from Medicare for up to two years.

analysis.who_pays: Physicians and practitioners who charge membership or incidental fees, or require purchases of non-covered items, as a condition of treating Medicare patients — they would lose that fee income and face sanctions, including possible exclusion from Medicare for up to two years, for violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Doctors charging Medicare patients extra fees

drawbacks.text: Physicians argue that Medicare does not pay for longer appointments and extra time with patients, so membership fees are how concierge practices fund services Medicare won't reimburse; banning the fees could push more doctors to leave Medicare entirely instead, leaving seniors with fewer doctors rather than more access.

The bill adds a new enforcement regime under which doctors can be excluded from Medicare for up to two years for charging a prohibited fee, which is a real compliance burden on practices even when the line between a covered service and an 'incidental' extra is murky.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it would have closed a specific loophole — seniors being charged extra fees to get services Medicare already covers — with sanctions capped at two years' exclusion from Medicare, a meaningful but not crushing penalty. The cost falls on physicians, and the strongest objection is that Medicare's low payment rates leave doctors few ways to fund longer visits and extra services, so a ban on membership fees might simply push more practices to stop taking Medicare altogether rather than make seniors better off. The bill never received a hearing, so that design question was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, each passed it down to a health subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Cardin introduced the bill on June 11, 2003, with four original cosponsors — Reps. Waxman, Brown of Ohio, Stark, and Kleczka.
The House referred it to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, on the day it was introduced.
In mid-June 2003 both committees referred it to their health subcommittees; the record shows no hearings, no markup, and no floor action at any point afterward.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians running concierge or membership-fee practices kept the freedom to charge Medicare patients extra fees for covered care, while seniors received no new protection against those charges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Physicians charging Medicare patients extra fees

for.name: Rep. Ben Cardin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on June 11, 2003.

for.name: Reps. Henry Waxman, Sherrod Brown, Fortney (Pete) Stark, and Gerald Kleczka
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair at the time: Rep. Billy Tauzin, R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health on June 19, 2003, and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair at the time: Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health on June 24, 2003, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All five members behind the bill were House Democrats and the Republican-controlled committees of referral never acted on it, but since it never reached a floor vote there is no roll-call showing how the parties actually split.

industries.industry: Physicians and medical practices (especially concierge and membership-based practices)
industries.note: The bill would have banned collecting membership or incidental fees from Medicare patients as a condition of treating them, cutting off fee income for practices that charge seniors extra for covered care. Its death left those practices free to keep charging.
